GOV.name: Governance & Liability
GOV.description: Management oversight, personal liability, and organizational governance
GOV.threatLandscape: Without clear governance, cybersecurity measures lack direction and accountability. Management that does not engage with security creates a culture of neglect, leaving the organization vulnerable to systematic failures.
GOV.bsiGuidance: BSI expects management to formally approve cybersecurity risk measures, appoint responsible persons, allocate adequate budget, and complete regular cybersecurity training (§38 BSIG). Personal liability applies to managing directors.

RSK.name: Risk Management
RSK.description: Risk identification, assessment, and treatment using an all-hazards approach (cyber, physical, environmental)
RSK.threatLandscape: Organizations that lack a structured risk assessment process cannot prioritize security investments effectively, leading to critical systems being left unprotected while resources are wasted on low-risk areas.
RSK.bsiGuidance: BSI expects a documented risk assessment methodology, complete risk register, treatment plan with management-approved risk acceptance, and regular review cycle (at least annual). Must cover all critical information systems using an all-hazards approach.

INC.name: Incident Handling
INC.threatLandscape: Cyber incidents are inevitable. Without a rehearsed response plan, organizations lose critical hours during the 24h BSI early warning window and the 72h notification deadline, risking regulatory penalties on top of operational damage.
INC.bsiGuidance: BSI expects an incident response plan with clear roles and escalation paths, 24h early warning capability (§32(1)), 72h incident notification with impact assessment, classification scheme, evidence of drills, and post-incident review process.

BCP.name: Business Continuity
BCP.threatLandscape: Ransomware and infrastructure failures can halt operations entirely. Without tested backup/recovery procedures and a crisis management plan, recovery times extend from hours to weeks, threatening business survival.
BCP.bsiGuidance: BSI expects a business impact analysis, documented BCP with RPO/RTO targets, regular backup and restore tests, crisis communication procedures, and evidence of at least annual BCP testing.

SUP.name: Supply Chain Security
SUP.threatLandscape: Supply chain attacks (SolarWinds, Kaseya) demonstrate that a single compromised supplier can cascade across thousands of organizations. Third-party risk is now a primary attack vector.
SUP.bsiGuidance: BSI expects a supplier register with security criticality classification, security requirements in contracts (SLAs, audit rights), ongoing supplier monitoring, incident notification clauses, and assessment of single points of failure.

PRO.name: Procurement & Development
PRO.description: Secure procurement, patch management, change control
PRO.threatLandscape: Unpatched vulnerabilities are the most common entry point for attackers. Organizations that lack structured vulnerability and patch management processes remain exposed to known exploits for weeks or months.
PRO.bsiGuidance: BSI expects security requirements in procurement, secure SDLC if developing software, vulnerability scanning and patching with defined SLAs, coordinated disclosure policy, configuration hardening baselines, and third-party component tracking.

EFF.name: Effectiveness Assessment
EFF.threatLandscape: Security measures degrade over time. Without regular effectiveness assessments, organizations develop a false sense of security while actual protection levels decline through configuration drift and evolving threats.
EFF.bsiGuidance: BSI expects defined KPIs/metrics for cybersecurity effectiveness, regular internal audits, management reviews, trend analysis of incidents and findings, and corrective action tracking from assessments.

TRN.name: Cyber Hygiene & Training
TRN.threatLandscape: Human error accounts for over 80% of security breaches. Phishing, social engineering, and credential misuse are the most effective attack techniques, all targeting untrained employees.
TRN.bsiGuidance: BSI expects a cybersecurity awareness training program for all employees, role-specific training for IT/security staff, training completion tracking, at least annual refresher courses, phishing simulations, and security onboarding for new employees.

CRY.name: Cryptography & Encryption
CRY.threatLandscape: Weak or outdated encryption exposes data in transit and at rest. Poor key management can render even strong encryption useless, and quantum computing threatens current cryptographic standards.
CRY.bsiGuidance: BSI expects a cryptography policy with approved algorithms (per BSI TR-02102), encryption of data at rest and in transit, key management procedures (generation, rotation, revocation), certificate management, and an inventory of cryptographic assets.

ACC.name: Access Control & HR Security
ACC.description: Identity management, privileged access, HR processes
ACC.threatLandscape: Excessive access rights are a multiplier for every other attack. A compromised account with broad privileges can access, exfiltrate, or destroy far more data than necessary. Insider threats exploit poor access controls.
ACC.bsiGuidance: BSI expects an access control policy based on least-privilege, user provisioning/de-provisioning process, regular access reviews, privileged access management (PAM), asset management policy, and HR security processes including joiners-movers-leavers.

AUT.name: Authentication & Communications
AUT.description: MFA or continuous authentication, secure communications, emergency channels
AUT.threatLandscape: Credential theft and password-only authentication are the primary vectors for account compromise. Without MFA, a single phished password grants full access. Insecure communications can be intercepted for espionage.
AUT.bsiGuidance: BSI expects multi-factor or continuous authentication for critical systems and remote access, secure voice/video/text communication solutions, emergency out-of-band communication channel, centralized identity management, and session management policies.

REG.name: Registration & Reporting
REG.description: BSI registration, annual updates, compliance evidence
REG.threatLandscape: Failure to register with BSI and maintain current contact data means the organization cannot receive threat warnings and cannot fulfill mandatory reporting obligations, compounding regulatory risk.
REG.bsiGuidance: BSI expects completed registration (§33), designated contact point, current registration data (annual update), compliance with information sharing obligations (§34), domain name registry maintenance (§39 if applicable), and documented regulatory correspondence.

DPA.name: Processor Agreements
DPA.description: Data Processing Agreements per GDPR Art. 28 with all processors handling personal data

ROP.name: Records of Processing
ROP.description: Documentation of every processing activity per GDPR Art. 30: purpose, legal basis, recipients, retention

TOM.name: Technical & Organisational Measures
TOM.description: Security measures protecting personal data per GDPR Art. 32

BRC.name: Breach Response
BRC.description: 72-hour notification process and breach documentation per GDPR Art. 33/34

DSR.name: Data Subject Rights
DSR.description: Workflow for handling access, erasure, portability, and objection requests within one month

ISMS.name: ISMS Mandatory Clauses
ISMS.description: ISO 27001:2022 clauses 4 to 10: context, leadership, planning, support, operation, evaluation, improvement
ISMS.threatLandscape: An undocumented or unscoped ISMS cannot be audited. Gaps in leadership commitment, risk planning, or documented information are the most common reasons organisations fail Stage 1 of an ISO 27001 audit.
ISMS.bsiGuidance: Mandatory clauses apply without exception. The auditor will verify: scope document, risk assessment methodology, IS policy signed by top management, documented roles, internal audit plan, management review records, and a continual improvement process.

ORG.name: Organizational Controls
ORG.description: Annex A.5: Policies, roles, supplier security, incident management, business continuity, and legal compliance
ORG.threatLandscape: Organizational controls are the governance layer. Without clear policies, defined roles, and supplier security requirements, technical controls have no mandate and no accountability, leaving gaps that attackers exploit.
ORG.bsiGuidance: Auditors look for evidence that policies are approved, communicated, and reviewed. Supplier agreements must include security clauses. Incident management must be planned before an incident occurs.

PPL.name: People Controls
PPL.description: Annex A.6: Screening, employment terms, awareness training, disciplinary process, remote working
PPL.threatLandscape: People are both the primary attack vector (phishing, social engineering) and the last line of defense. Untrained staff and poor offboarding are among the most commonly exploited weaknesses.
PPL.bsiGuidance: Evidence required: background check process, signed confidentiality agreements, annual security awareness training completion records, remote working policy.

PHY.name: Physical Controls
PHY.description: Annex A.7: Physical perimeters, entry controls, equipment protection, secure disposal
PHY.threatLandscape: Physical access to systems bypasses all logical controls. Unsecured offices, unlocked screens, and improper equipment disposal are frequently exploited, often by opportunistic threats, not sophisticated attackers.
PHY.bsiGuidance: For a remote-first company using co-working spaces, physical controls focus on: clear desk policy, screen lock, off-premises asset security, and secure disposal of laptops and storage media.

TEC.name: Technological Controls
TEC.description: Annex A.8: Endpoint security, access rights, vulnerability management, cryptography, logging, change management
TEC.threatLandscape: The largest Annex A section (34 controls). Technological gaps (unpatched systems, misconfigured cloud resources, missing MFA, inadequate logging) are the root cause of the majority of security incidents.
TEC.bsiGuidance: Auditors check that controls are actually implemented, not just documented. Expect technical evidence: configuration screenshots, patch logs, SIEM outputs, backup restore test results, and access review records.

AI-LIT.name: AI Literacy
AI-LIT.description: Ensure staff and persons operating AI systems on the company's behalf have a sufficient level of AI literacy.
AI-LIT.threatLandscape: Untrained staff using AI tools cause data leakage, hallucination-driven errors, and deepfake exposure that organisations cannot defend in audit or court.

AI-PRO.name: Prohibited Practices
AI-PRO.description: Screen AI use cases against the eight (plus one) banned practices in Art. 5 and document the screening outcome.
AI-PRO.threatLandscape: Using a prohibited practice triggers the highest penalty tier (EUR 35M or 7% of global turnover) regardless of intent.

AI-INV.name: AI System Inventory
AI-INV.description: Maintain an inventory of every AI system in use, classify each by risk tier, and re-classify on substantial modification.
AI-INV.threatLandscape: Without an inventory, shadow-AI deployments evade oversight and create unmitigated compliance and liability exposure.

AI-RSK.name: AI Risk Management
AI-RSK.description: Operate a documented risk management system for high-risk AI systems, with annual review and treatment of identified risks.
AI-RSK.threatLandscape: Unmanaged AI risks (bias, drift, robustness failures) translate directly into incident exposure under Art. 73.

AI-FRI.name: Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment
AI-FRI.description: Conduct a Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment before deploying high-risk AI systems in public, financial, or insurance contexts.
AI-FRI.threatLandscape: Skipping the FRIA exposes the deployer to civil claims from affected persons and to market-surveillance enforcement.

AI-OVS.name: Human Oversight
AI-OVS.description: Designate a competent human overseer per high-risk AI system and verify oversight effectiveness annually.
AI-OVS.threatLandscape: Autonomous high-risk AI systems without effective human override breach Art. 14 and create direct provider/deployer liability.

AI-TRA.name: Transparency
AI-TRA.description: Disclose AI interactions and AI-generated content to end users; watermark synthetic content; disclose deepfakes.
AI-TRA.threatLandscape: Lack of disclosure on chatbots and synthetic content breaches Art. 50 and undermines trust with customers and regulators.

AI-INC.name: AI Incident Reporting
AI-INC.description: Document the AI incident response procedure; notify the market surveillance authority of serious incidents within 15 days.
AI-INC.threatLandscape: Failure to notify within the 15-day window triggers the second penalty tier (EUR 15M or 3% of turnover).

AI-DOC.name: Technical Documentation
AI-DOC.description: Maintain Annex IV technical documentation, automatic logging, and the EU Declaration of Conformity for high-risk AI systems.
AI-DOC.legalBasis: Art. 11, 12, 18, 19, 47 · Annex IV, V EU AI Act
AI-DOC.threatLandscape: Incomplete technical documentation prevents conformity assessment and blocks placing on the EU market.

AI-GPI.name: General-Purpose AI
AI-GPI.description: GPAI provider obligations: model card, copyright policy, training-content summary, plus systemic-risk evaluation when training compute exceeds 10^25 FLOPs.
AI-GPI.threatLandscape: GPAI providers that miss transparency obligations face EU AI Office enforcement directly, with fines under Art. 101.

CRA-MFG.name: Manufacturer Obligations
CRA-MFG.description: Per-product cybersecurity risk assessment and management body sign-off before placing the product on the EU market.
CRA-MFG.threatLandscape: Manufacturers that ship without a documented risk assessment have no defence when actively exploited vulnerabilities surface.

CRA-ESS.name: Essential Cybersecurity Requirements
CRA-ESS.description: Compliance with Annex I Part I: no known exploitable vulnerabilities at placing on market, secure by default, protection of data confidentiality, integrity, availability.
CRA-ESS.legalBasis: Annex I Part I EU CRA
CRA-ESS.threatLandscape: Products that fail essential requirements cannot legally remain on the EU market and trigger the highest penalty tier.

CRA-VLN.name: Vulnerability Handling
CRA-VLN.description: Documented vulnerability handling, coordinated disclosure policy, security updates without delay, and public disclosure of fixed vulnerabilities.
CRA-VLN.legalBasis: Annex I Part II EU CRA
CRA-VLN.threatLandscape: Vendors without a vulnerability handling process cannot meet the 24h / 72h / 14-day reporting cascade and become liable for downstream incidents.

CRA-INC.name: Active Exploitation Reporting
CRA-INC.description: 24-hour early warning to ENISA and CSIRT, 72-hour notification, 14-day final report for actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents.
CRA-INC.threatLandscape: Missed reporting deadlines (other than the 24h deadline for SMEs) trigger the highest penalty tier and product-recall powers.

CRA-CONF.name: Conformity Assessment
CRA-CONF.description: Conformity assessment route per product class (self-assessment Module A, Module B+C with notified body, or Module H quality system) followed by CE marking.
CRA-CONF.threatLandscape: Products without valid conformity assessment cannot be placed on the EU market from 11 December 2027.

CRA-DOC.name: Technical Documentation
CRA-DOC.description: Maintain Annex VII technical documentation for each product placed on the EU market.
CRA-DOC.threatLandscape: Missing or incomplete technical documentation blocks market surveillance verification and triggers product withdrawal.

CRA-SUP.name: Support Period
CRA-SUP.description: Publicly commit to a security update support period (default five years or expected product life, whichever is longer).
CRA-SUP.threatLandscape: Failure to support the full period exposes the manufacturer to claims from customers stranded on insecure products.

CRA-SBOM.name: Software Bill of Materials
CRA-SBOM.description: Generate and maintain a machine-readable Software Bill of Materials for each product placed on the EU market.
CRA-SBOM.legalBasis: Annex I Part II §1 EU CRA
CRA-SBOM.threatLandscape: Without an SBOM, manufacturers cannot trace which products contain a vulnerable component and miss the Art. 14 reporting window.

CRA-IMP.name: Importer and Distributor
CRA-IMP.description: Importers verify manufacturer compliance before placing on market; distributors perform due diligence on conformity markings.
CRA-IMP.threatLandscape: Importers and distributors that miss verification inherit manufacturer liability under Art. 22.

CRA-OSS.name: Open-Source Steward
CRA-OSS.description: Open-source software stewards adopt a cybersecurity policy, coordinated vulnerability disclosure, and report actively exploited vulnerabilities.
CRA-OSS.threatLandscape: OSS stewards are penalty-exempt under Art. 64(10), but downstream commercial users still depend on their reporting.

DPO.description: Assessment of the designation duty under §38 BDSG and Art. 37 GDPR, and the position and tasks of the person designated
